newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian opposition head could be unifying leader.
newsitem.headline: Albanian opposition head could be unifying leader.

text.p: Albanian Socialist leader Fatos Nano has emerged as a possible head of state who could unite the anarchic country if right-wing President Sali Berisha bows to growing demands that he quit.

Nano was released from jail by the new all-party government as armed unrest swept the country earlier this month and pardoned by Berisha of corruption charges that put him behind bars for nearly four years.
He was among the first Albanian thinkers to publish articles openly questioning the communist orthodoxies of one-party rule and a centralised economy, in 1990 before the collapse of communism.

In his first news conference since his release on Thursday the 44-year-old economist, head of the ex-communist Socialists who were the main opposition under the previous right-wing Democratic government, indicated Berisha should step aside.
"I would prefer to shake hands with him as an Albanian citizen and not as President," he said.
Nano was jailed for 12 years in 1994 after he was charged with being implicated in an Italian aid scandal during his brief stint as prime minister in Albania's last communist administration in 1991.
The opposition has maintained that the charges were politically inspired, and several international human rights groups including Amnesty International have campaigned for his release.

Describing his time in prison on Monday, he said he was isolated and his every move strictly controlled, but conditions were better than those during the Stalinist dictatorship of the late Enver Hoxha.
"It was a constant challenge," he told a news conference. "But I was only deprived of my physical freedom, I didn't lose anything else."

Many Albanians believe Nano could become a rallying point for the country, divided into a south controlled by armed rebels calling for Berisha's resignation and the north where law and order is shaky after similar mass looting of weapons from army barracks.
The Socialist leader is untainted by the scandal over fraudulent pyramid savings schemes that collapsed earlier this year, bankrupting thousands of families, as he was in jail when they flourished.

Rebels in the south who rose against the former government in fury over the failed schemes blame the president for allowing them to flourish, and for not warning people of the risk to their investments.

Nano's Socialists were ousted by Berisha's Democrats by a landslide in 1992, but gained ground in local elections four months later and were shown to have wide support in 1994 when a new Democratic draft constitution was rejected in a referendum by voters angry at government corruption and inefficiency.

The Democrats won again in another landslide in elections last summer, but the polls were boycotted by the opposition amid charges of vote-rigging and intimidation and branded as seriously flawed by international monitors.
Fatos Nano was born in Tirana on September 16, 1952 -- his father was a journalist who became head of state Radio and TV -- and studied political economics at Tirana University.

After three years as an economist at a steel works in Elbasan, central Albania, he returned to Tirana to work in the Institute of Marxist-Leninist studies, a communist think-tank headed by Hoxha's widow.
During this time he also worked part-time as an economist at an agricultural cooperative and as a professor of economics at the university.
When communist rule ended Nano, who sports a neatly-trimmed beard and glasses, was appointed secretary-general of the Council of Ministers, the cabinet.
He became a deputy Prime Minister in January 1991, and a month later took over as premier.
Nano, who speaks English, French and Italian and has a working knowledge of several Slav languages, is married with a 19-year-old son and a 16-year-old daughter.

One current obstacle to Nano taking power is a controversial law introduced by Berisha in 1995 barring all those in positions of authority during the communist era from standing for public office until 2002.
Nano called for the law to be overturned once normal life was restored in the country.
